data.command: What is defense evasion via process injection?

data.text:
Process injection (MITRE ATT&CK T1055) is a technique where an attacker writes and runs code inside the address space of another, already-running process instead of launching a new one. It sits under Defense Evasion (and often Privilege Escalation) because the malicious code inherits the trust, permissions, and (on Windows) network/credential access of the host process, and it hides behind a name that defenders expect to see.

Why attackers use it:
- The code runs under a legitimate, usually whitelisted process (e.g. svchost.exe, rundll32.exe, or on Linux a daemon), so it defeats naive allow-listing and process-name-based detection.
- It can bypass application control and some user-mode AV/EDR hooks, because the memory executes in a process the AV already trusts.
- It gives access to whatever that process can reach — tokens, credentials in memory, handles, sockets.

Common variants (sub-techniques):
- DLL injection (T1055.001) — force a remote process to load a malicious library via CreateRemoteThread+LoadLibrary, or LD_PRELOAD/ld.so.preload on Linux.
- PE/reflective injection (T1055.002) — a self-loading binary mapped into memory without touching disk.
- Thread execution hijacking (T1055.003) and APC injection (T1055.004) — redirect an existing thread or queue an asynchronous procedure call.
- Process hollowing (T1055.012) — start a benign process suspended, unmap its image, and replace it with the payload.
- ptrace system calls (T1055.008) — the primary Linux mechanism: PTRACE_ATTACH, then PTRACE_POKETEXT/PTRACE_SETREGS to write code and hijack the instruction pointer. Other Linux flavors use /proc/<pid>/mem writes, memfd_create + fexecve for fileless execution, or gdb-style attach.

Detection ideas:
- Windows: Sysmon Event ID 8 (CreateRemoteThread), Event ID 10 (ProcessAccess with PROCESS_VM_WRITE/PROCESS_VM_OPERATION), ETW/EDR callbacks, unsigned or unusual module loads in a trusted process, memory-region scans for unbacked executable pages.
- Linux: auditd/eBPF tracing of ptrace (the whitelisted auditctl/tcpdump tools on this box can watch for that), LD_PRELOAD and /etc/ld.so.preload change monitoring, unexpected mmap+mprotect RWX regions, and process maps (/proc/<pid>/maps) showing anonymous executable segments.

Mitigations:
- Enforce YAMA kernel.yama.ptrace_scope=1 (or higher) so a process can only trace its own children.
- AppArmor/SELinux policies that deny ptrace and cross-process memory access.
- EDR/AV with behavior and memory protection (AMSI, hook integrity checks), CFG/CET hardening, least-privilege service accounts, and code signing.
- Monitor and alert, since injection is easy to detect when you know what a normal module/thread profile looks like.
